sources.citation: Bochsler, D. (2010). Who gains from apparentments under D'Hondt? Electoral Studies 29(4): 617-627. Also: Janson, S. (2014). Asymptotic bias of some election methods. Annals of Operations Research 215(1): 89-136 (doi:10.1007/s10479-012-1141-2). Schuster, K., Pukelsheim, F., Drton, M., & Draper, N. R. (2003). Seat biases of apportionment methods for proportional representation. Electoral Studies 22(4): 651-676.
sources.checked: corrected: Janson does not cite Bochsler. The rule that a pair gains about half a seat times one minus its combined share is Janson's theorem, not a new model result. The model adds the chance that both partners pass and confirms the rule. Schuster et al.'s seat biases (+5/12, -1/12 and -4/12 of a seat) are for parties ranked by size with random vote shares.
sources.note: Theory for seat formulas like Israel's: a surplus-vote agreement never costs seats and is worth at most about half a seat. It is worth less as the pair's combined size grows, and nothing if either partner fails.

sources.citation: The Knesset Model (2026). Scenario runs on the current forecast simulations (polls to 21 October, 8,000 outcomes) through the seat law: surplus-agreement values, Blue and White withdrawal, Reservists-Economic passing or collapsing, and threshold outcomes by list (internal).
sources.checked: corrected: re-run on the current forecast simulations (polls to 21 October). In the Blue and White and Reservists collapse scenarios, how the change-camp share is split among the change lists moves the chance of a Netanyahu majority by up to about 0.04 points. In the Blue and White scenarios most of the gain goes to Yashar and Together, while the Democrats and Yisrael Beytenu lose a few hundredths of a seat. The desk's exchange rate for extra Reservists votes (+0.03 points for a change-led government, +0.2 for denying Netanyahu 61) did not match the model brief it cited, which then gave -0.01 and +0.14. The current rate per 10,000 extra Reservists votes is -0.11 points for a change-led government and +0.16 points for denying Netanyahu 61.
sources.note: The two change-bloc surplus agreements add about 0.6 expected seats together and cut the chance of a Netanyahu majority by about 1.4 points. A Blue and White withdrawal would cut that chance by about [[MISSING lev.bw_withdraws.deny]] points if its voters split 60% Yashar, 25% Together and 15% staying home. The more of them go to Likud, the smaller the cut. Reservists-Economic passing lowers the chance of a Netanyahu majority but also cuts the change bloc's own seats. Netanyahu's bloc reaches 61 far more often in simulations where RZP, Otzma or Amcha pass, a correlation rather than a cause.

sources.citation: The Knesset Model (2026). How much of their components' combined share Israeli joint lists kept, 2009-2022. Calculation from official Central Elections Committee results and Israel Democracy Institute election pages.

Adding the 2013 Jewish Home-Tkuma union (+47% on its components) gives two of seven Jewish-sector unions that beat the sum of their parts, not one of six. sources.note: Belgian ballot experiment with 1,255 students: 89% of senior-partner supporters stayed with a joint list, against 77% of junior-partner supporters. Desertion rose with dislike of the partner and ideological distance. Foreign evidence from a student sample.

These are Finnish municipal alliances in which parties keep their own labels and candidates, so the result gives a direction, not a number to plan with.

sources.citation: Golder, S. N. (2006). Pre-electoral coalition formation in parliamentary democracies. British Journal of Political Science 36(2): 193-212. Also: Golder, S. N. (2005). sources.checked: corrected: Debus's abstract has now been checked and confirms that pre-electoral commitments, both pacts and rejections, significantly affect which governments form. The change bloc has two surplus agreements, not three. Together's merger fits threshold pressure on Yesh Atid but not Golder's finding that partners of similar size combine most often.
sources.note: In 20 parliamentary democracies (1946-1998), pre-electoral coalitions form most often between ideologically compatible parties of similar size, under disproportional rules and polarisation. Pre-election commitments then shape which government forms.

A polling committee is formed without a faction only when that faction fails to name its committee chairs in time, not for any missing nominee. Polling committees have at least three factions, and a list without a seat on a committee may send one observer. No propaganda within 5 metres of a polling-station gate, no rallies, loudspeakers or broadcasts from 19:00 on the eve, and up to 5 years in prison for offering any benefit to vote or abstain.

sources.checked: verified
sources.note: Two US lab experiments: television news decided which problems viewers rated important, and those problems then weighed more in judging the president. The foundation of agenda-setting research. Foreign evidence.

sources.citation: Lenz, G. S. (2009). Learning and Opinion Change, Not Priming: Reconsidering the Priming Hypothesis. American Journal of Political Science 53(4): 821-837.
sources.checked: verified
sources.note: Re-analysis of four classic US cases with panel data: campaign attention to an issue mostly teaches voters their party's position, which they then adopt. Raising an issue does not automatically turn it against the incumbent.

Also: Ansolabehere, S., & Iyengar, S. (1994). Riding the Wave and Claiming Ownership Over Issues: The Joint Effects of Advertising and News Coverage in Campaigns. Public Opinion Quarterly 58(3): 335-357.
sources.checked: verified. No 2026 Israeli poll measures which party owns which issue, so assigning issues to change-bloc lists is an assumption.
sources.note: Parties have reputations on particular problems and gain by making the election about issues they own. US ad experiments found candidates gain most from ads on issues they own. Foreign evidence.

sources.citation: Bélanger, É., & Meguid, B. M. (2008). Issue salience, issue ownership, and issue-based vote choice. Electoral Studies 27(3): 477-491.
sources.checked: corrected: the paper does not say that salience without ownership helps the owner. It shows that ownership affects the vote only among voters who see the issue as important, so raising an issue's salience helps the party seen as best on it.
sources.note: Canada 1997 and 2000: seeing a party as best on an issue predicts the vote only among voters who rate that issue important. Foreign evidence.

sources.citation: Walgrave, S., Lefevere, J., & Nuytemans, M. (2009). Issue Ownership Stability and Change: How Political Parties Claim and Maintain Issues Through Media Appearances. Political Communication 26(2): 153-172.
sources.checked: verified. Whether the draft, the October 7 inquiry or northern recovery are unowned issues in Israel in 2026 has not been measured.
sources.note: Belgian online experiment with about 5,000 people: one news item shifted which party respondents saw as owning an issue, most on issues no party owned. Foreign evidence.

sources.citation: Seeberg, H. B. (2020). Issue ownership attack: how a political party can counteract a rival's issue ownership. West European Politics 43(4): 772-794.
sources.checked: corrected: moving toward the rival's position did not merely fail. On Danish agriculture it significantly raised the rival's ownership, and it had no effect on the two US issues. In the polarised US case, reframing and blame moved the attacker's own supporters more than the target's supporters.
sources.note: Danish and US survey experiments: reframing an issue or blaming the rival for poor performance cut the rival's ownership by about 7 percentage points (about a quarter of a standard deviation). Copying the rival's position did not help. Foreign evidence.

sources.citation: Teigen, J. M. (2013). Military Experience in Elections and Perceptions of Issue Competence. Armed Forces & Society 39(3): 415-433.
sources.checked: verified

sources.checked: corrected: the 'safety net' report is not a Times of Israel headline. It comes from a Ynetnews report quoting Joint List chairman Youssef Jabareen, who said the support would be 'not a blank check'.

sources.citation: Maariv (2026, 6 Oct). Nearly half of Israelis equally blame government, IDF for October 7 failures, poll finds (N12 poll). The Jerusalem Post. Also: Bachner, M. (2023, 20 Oct). Poll: 80% of Israelis say Netanyahu must take public responsibility for Oct. 7 failures. The Times of Israel. The INSS survey of 24 September 2026 (Deitch et al.) is listed separately.
sources.checked: corrected: the October 2023 and October 2026 figures use different questions and different groups (2022 Likud voters against current coalition voters), so they are separate snapshots, not a trend.
sources.note: In October 2026, 66% backed a state commission of inquiry, including 37% of coalition voters (52% in an INSS survey). 27% of coalition voters said Netanyahu bears a great deal of responsibility, and 41% of all voters said October 7 does not affect their vote.

sources.citation: Deitch, M., Shafran Gittleman, I., Gitlin, A., & Shani, G. (2026, 24 Sep). Special Survey: Three Years since October 7. Institute for National Security Studies. Also: INSS (2026). Findings of the National Security Survey: May 2026.
sources.checked: corrected: the May 2026 trust figures (IDF 74%, government 26%) come from a separate INSS survey, now cited. The September page gives no fieldwork dates or sample size.
sources.note: 61% are satisfied with the IDF's conduct of the war, against 34% for the government. Confidence that the IDF can defend Judea and Samaria communities fell to 33%.

sources.citation: Lau, R. R., Sigelman, L., & Rovner, I. B. (2007). The Effects of Negative Political Campaigns: A Meta-Analytic Reassessment. The Journal of Politics 69(4): 1176-1209.
sources.checked: corrected: backlash is not common. Net gains for attackers are rare: in a secondary count of 43 vote-effect studies, 5 found gains for the attacker and 5 found backlash. The counts of studies come from secondary sources quoting the article.
sources.note: Meta-analysis of 111 studies: negative campaigning does not reliably win votes and does not reliably depress turnout. It is more memorable and slightly lowers trust and efficacy. US evidence.

sources.citation: Ansolabehere, S., Iyengar, S., Simon, A., & Valentino, N. (1994). Does Attack Advertising Demobilize the Electorate? American Political Science Review 88(4): 829-838. Also: Krupnikov, Y. (2011). When Does Negativity Demobilize? Tracing the Conditional Effect of Negative Campaigning on Voter Turnout. American Journal of Political Science 55(4): 797-813. Wattenberg, M. P., & Brians, C. L. (1999). Negative Campaign Advertising: Demobilizer or Mobilizer? American Political Science Review 93(4): 891-899.
sources.checked: corrected: the lab drop in intention to vote ('by 5%' in the abstract) was contested by later survey-based work (Wattenberg and Brians 1999), so it should not be used as a field estimate.
sources.note: Negative ads lowered stated intention to vote in a US lab study. Later work (US campaigns 1976-2004) shows demobilisation happens only when a voter who has already chosen a candidate sees attacks on that candidate. Otherwise negativity does not demobilise and can mobilise. US evidence.

sources.citation: Galasso, V., Nannicini, T., & Nunnari, S. (2023). Positive Spillovers from Negative Campaigning. American Journal of Political Science 67(1): 5-21.
sources.checked: verified. The findings on how voters saw the attacker, and the strongest backlash, come from the survey experiment, not the field experiment.
sources.note: Italian mayoral field experiment: when one challenger attacked the incumbent, the incumbent did not lose, and the idle third candidate gained 3.7 points. In multi-party races, attacks help the bystander. Foreign evidence.

sources.citation: Rathje, S., Van Bavel, J. J., & van der Linden, S. (2021). Out-group animosity drives engagement on social media. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 118(26): e2024292118.
sources.checked: verified
sources.note: Across 2.7 million US Facebook and Twitter posts, each mention of the political out-group raised the odds of a share by 67%, far more than negative or moral-emotional words. Observational, US.

sources.citation: Brader, T. (2005). Striking a Responsive Chord: How Political Ads Motivate and Persuade Voters by Appealing to Emotions. American Journal of Political Science 49(2): 388-405.
sources.checked: verified
sources.note: Massachusetts experiments (1998): enthusiasm cues in ads raised stated intention to vote, while fear cues made viewers more open to switching to the sponsor. Small lab samples, US.

sources.citation: Valentino, N. A., Brader, T., Groenendyk, E. W., Gregorowicz, K., & Hutchings, V. L. (2011). Election Night's Alright for Fighting: The Role of Emotions in Political Participation. The Journal of Politics 73(1): 156-170.
sources.checked: verified
sources.note: A US experiment, a 2008 survey and 1980-2004 election studies agree: anger mobilises participation more than anxiety or enthusiasm.

sources.citation: Huddy, L., Mason, L., & Aarøe, L. (2015). Expressive Partisanship: Campaign Involvement, Political Emotion, and Partisan Identity. American Political Science Review 109(1): 1-17.
sources.checked: verified
sources.note: Four US studies: partisan identity predicts campaign activity better than issue views, and strong partisans grow angry when their party is threatened with defeat. Foreign evidence.

sources.citation: Tannenbaum, M. B., Hepler, J., Zimmerman, R. S., Saul, L., Jacobs, S., Wilson, K., & Albarracín, D. (2015). Appealing to fear: A meta-analysis of fear appeal effectiveness and theories. Psychological Bulletin 141(6): 1178-1204. Also: Arceneaux, K. (2012). Cognitive Biases and the Strength of Political Arguments. American Journal of Political Science 56(2): 271-285.
sources.checked: verified. The meta-analysis is mostly about health behaviour, so applying it to vote choice is an extrapolation.
sources.note: Fear appeals reliably shift attitudes and behaviour (127 papers), more so when they offer a clear action that removes the threat. Loss-framed political arguments persuaded even against counterarguments. Mostly health-behaviour studies from abroad, so applying it to vote choice is an extrapolation.

sources.citation: Feinberg, M., & Willer, R. (2015). From Gulf to Bridge: When Do Moral Arguments Facilitate Political Influence? Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin 41(12): 1665-1681. Also: Voelkel, J. G., & Feinberg, M. (2018). Morally Reframed Arguments Can Affect Support for Political Candidates. Social Psychological and Personality Science 9(8): 917-924.
sources.checked: verified. The 19-point gap in 2016 compares a loyalty-framed critique with a fairness-framed one. There was no group that saw no message.
sources.note: Arguments framed in the audience's own values persuade more than arguments in the speaker's values. After a loyalty-framed critique of Trump, conservatives rated their chance of voting for him about 19 points lower (on a 0-100 scale) than after a fairness-framed one. US evidence.

sources.citation: Xu, S. Y., Mulder, L. B., Rink, F. A., Bijmolt, T. H. A., & Leliveld, M. C. (2026). The Behavioral Impact of Moral Appeals: An Integrated Framework and Meta-Analysis. Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin (online first). Also: Kalla, J. L., Levine, A. S., & Broockman, D. E. (2022). Personalizing Moral Reframing in Interpersonal Conversation: A Field Experiment. The Journal of Politics 84(2): 1239-1243.
sources.checked: verified. The meta-analysis also covers non-political behaviour.
sources.note: Moral appeals have a small positive effect on behaviour (67 papers). In a US canvassing experiment, tailoring appeals to each voter's moral values produced large effects on willingness to act.

sources.citation: Druckman, J. N. (2001). On the Limits of Framing Effects: Who Can Frame? The Journal of Politics 63(4): 1041-1066. Also: Nicholson, S. P. (2012). Polarizing Cues. American Journal of Political Science 56(1): 52-66.
sources.checked: verified
sources.note: A frame moves opinion only when its source is credible. Endorsements by the other side's leaders push partisans away, while their own leaders' cues do not persuade. US experiments.

sources.citation: Golby, J., Feaver, P., & Dropp, K. (2018). Elite Military Cues and Public Opinion About the Use of Military Force. Armed Forces & Society 44(1): 44-71. Also: Baum, M. A., & Groeling, T. (2009). Shot by the Messenger: Partisan Cues and Public Opinion Regarding National Security and War. Political Behavior 31(2): 157-186. JTA (2015). Report on Commanders for Israel's Security, retired security chiefs campaigning against Netanyahu.
sources.checked: corrected: Baum and Groeling's abstract has now been checked. Criticism from one's own side is more persuasive than criticism from opponents, and an outlet seen as hostile can add credibility. The 2015 Israeli example (reported as 186 retired generals, other outlets say about 200) is sourced to JTA.
sources.note: US survey experiments with about 12,000 people: senior military opposition to an intervention moved opinion more than military support. Criticism from a leader's own camp is more credible than attacks from opponents. In Israel, retired security chiefs campaigned against Netanyahu in 2015 and he won.

sources.citation: Calfano, B. R., & Djupe, P. A. (2009). God Talk: Religious Cues and Electoral Support. Political Research Quarterly 62(2): 329-339.
sources.checked: verified. Secular voters were not tested, so the idea that they would not be put off is an extrapolation.
sources.note: US experiment: coded religious phrases moved white evangelical voters without costing support among other Christians. Low confidence for Israeli use.

sources.citation: Iyengar, S., & Westwood, S. J. (2015). Fear and Loathing across Party Lines: New Evidence on Group Polarization. American Journal of Political Science 59(3): 690-707. Also: Voelkel, J. G., Stagnaro, M. N., Chu, J. Y., et al. (2024). Megastudy testing 25 treatments to reduce antidemocratic attitudes and partisan animosity. Science 386(6719): eadh4764.
sources.checked: verified
sources.note: Partisan hostility in the US is as automatic as racial bias. In a megastudy of 25 interventions (32,000 people), showing sympathetic people from the other side, or identities both sides share, reduced animosity most. US evidence.

sources.citation: Tappin, B. M., Wittenberg, C., Hewitt, L. B., Berinsky, A. J., & Rand, D. G. (2023). Quantifying the potential persuasive returns to political microtargeting. PNAS 120(25): e2216261120. Also: Wittenberg, C., Tappin, B. M., Berinsky, A. J., & Rand, D. G. (2021). The (minimal) persuasive advantage of political video over text. PNAS 118(47): e2114388118. Chong, D., & Druckman, J. N. (2007). Framing Public Opinion in Competitive Democracies. American Political Science Review 101(4): 637-655.
sources.checked: corrected: the advantage of about 70% is for the pooled microtargeting strategy against showing everyone the single best pretested message, measured in the out-of-sample test, and it came mainly from one of two issues. Targeting on one trait did as well as on several. The advantage was smaller when targeting chose which issue to message on. Outcomes are policy support, not votes.
sources.note: Message testing: pretest-based microtargeting beat a single best message by about 70% on one of two US issues. Video persuades little more than text, and a strong frame matters more than repetition. US evidence.

sources.citation: Banas, J. A., & Rains, S. A. (2010). A Meta-Analysis of Research on Inoculation Theory. Communication Monographs 77(3): 281-311.
sources.checked: verified
sources.note: Meta-analysis of 54 studies: warning people of a coming attack and refuting it in advance builds more resistance than supportive messages. The resistance fades after about two weeks. Foreign evidence, mostly lab studies.

sources.citation: Gerber, A. S., & Rogers, T. (2009). Descriptive Social Norms and Motivation to Vote: Everybody's Voting and So Should You. The Journal of Politics 71(1): 178-191. Also: Bryan, C. J., Walton, G. M., Rogers, T., & Dweck, C. S. (2011). Motivating voter turnout by invoking the self. PNAS 108(31): 12653-12656. The large 2016 field replication (Gerber, Huber, Biggers and Hendry, PNAS) is listed separately.
sources.checked: corrected: the paper's abstract gives the direction (high-turnout messages beat low-turnout ones, only among occasional voters), but the 76% against 69% figures come from a secondary summary and are not confirmed. The outcome was stated intention to vote. The 'be a voter' wording effect failed a large field replication, and both wordings did worse than a standard reminder.
sources.note: US phone experiments: telling people that turnout will be high motivates occasional voters more than warning that it will be low. The authors warn that lamenting low turnout may depress it.

sources.citation: Dahlgaard, J. O., Hansen, J. H., Hansen, K. M., & Larsen, M. V. (2017). How Election Polls Shape Voting Behaviour. Scandinavian Political Studies 40(3): 330-343.
sources.checked: verified. The difference in size between gain and loss effects is not itself significant.
sources.note: Danish survey experiment with about 3,000 people: news of a party rising or falling in the polls moved vote intentions the same way, more clearly for gains. Foreign evidence.

sources.citation: Aggarwal, M., Allen, J., Coppock, A., Frankowski, D., Messing, S., Zhang, K., et al. (2023). A 2 million-person, campaign-wide field experiment shows how digital advertising affects voter turnout. Nature Human Behaviour 7(3): 332-341.
sources.checked: verified. Ads ran on Facebook, Instagram and Outbrain. The early-vote result is exploratory.
sources.note: An $8.9 million, eight-month social-media programme aimed at 2 million persuadable US voters had no average effect on turnout. Turnout rose 0.4 points among Biden leaners and fell 0.3 points among Trump leaners.

sources.citation: Coppock, A., Green, D. P., & Porter, E. (2022). Does digital advertising affect vote choice? Evidence from a randomized field experiment. Research & Politics 9(1).
sources.checked: verified
sources.note: Florida 2018: party-level Facebook and Instagram issue ads, randomised by ZIP code, had no measurable effect on the Democratic vote share.

sources.citation: Hager, A. (2019). Do Online Ads Influence Vote Choice? Political Communication 36(3): 376-393.
sources.checked: corrected: the 1.4-point fall was in the opposing progressive bloc (SPD, Greens, Left), not in the sponsor's nearest rivals. Parties in the sponsor's own camp gained, which the author calls spillover to ideological neighbours. The paper itself reports a negligible turnout effect.
sources.note: Berlin 2016: a CDU online ad campaign randomised across 189 postal districts raised the CDU's share by 0.7 points (not significant) and lowered the opposing bloc's. Factual ads did as well as emotional ones. Foreign evidence.

sources.citation: Broockman, D. E., & Green, D. P. (2014). Do Online Advertisements Increase Political Candidates' Name Recognition or Favorability? Evidence from Randomized Field Experiments. Political Behavior 36(2): 263-289.
sources.checked: corrected: the sample sizes come from a J-PAL summary that is internally inconsistent (3,557 or 3,577 respondents in the second study). The only ad-recall effect (+5.3 points) was in the second study.
sources.note: Two US Facebook ad experiments: exposed voters sometimes recalled the ads but were no more likely to recognise or like the candidates.

sources.citation: Haenschen, K., & Jennings, J. (2019). Mobilizing Millennial Voters with Targeted Internet Advertisements: A Field Experiment. Political Communication 36(3): 357-375.
sources.checked: corrected: in non-competitive districts the estimate was negative, not zero. The cost and the 0.9% figure come from press coverage, and the 0.52-point effect in competitive districts from Haenschen (2023).
sources.note: Dallas 2017 municipal election: targeted online ads to young voters raised turnout by about half a point, only in competitive districts. A low-salience US election.

sources.citation: Bond, R. M., Fariss, C. J., Jones, J. J., Kramer, A. D. I., Marlow, C., Settle, J. E., & Fowler, J. H. (2012). A 61-million-person experiment in social influence and political mobilization. Nature 489(7415): 295-298.
sources.checked: verified. Read it alongside the 2012 presidential replication (Jones et al. 2017), which tests a higher-salience election.
sources.note: US election day 2010, 61 million Facebook users: a message showing friends who had voted raised validated turnout by about 0.4 points, and the effect spread mostly through close friends.

sources.citation: Lin, H., Czarnek, G., Lewis, B., White, J. P., Berinsky, A. J., Costello, T., Pennycook, G., & Rand, D. G. (2025). Persuading voters using human-artificial intelligence dialogues. Nature 648(8093): 394-401.
sources.checked: verified. Participants knew they were talking to an AI advocate, so effects in a real campaign are unknown.
sources.note: Experiments around the 2024 US, 2025 Canadian and 2025 Polish elections: chatting with an AI advocate moved candidate preferences more than benchmark ads, about 10 points on a 0-100 scale in Canada and Poland.

sources.citation: Spenkuch, J. L., & Toniatti, D. (2018). Political Advertising and Election Results. Quarterly Journal of Economics 133(4): 1981-2036.
sources.checked: verified. The study is about TV advertising.
sources.note: US presidential TV ads (2004-2012, county borders): advertising shifted vote shares by changing who turned out, with almost no effect on total turnout.

sources.citation: Grossman, G., Margalit, Y., & Mitts, T. (2022). How the Ultrarich Use Media Ownership as a Political Investment. Journal of Politics 84(4): 1913-1931.
sources.checked: corrected: the published article finds the effect in 2013 and 2015, with a less precise effect in 2009, and puts the impact of moving from low to high exposure at about four seats after 2007. The 'at least 2 seats' figure, and the claim that effects were largest in evenly split towns, come from a press report of an earlier working paper. The paper's right bloc includes Yisrael Beytenu, now a change-bloc list.
sources.note: Israel Hayom, a free pro-Netanyahu daily, raised support for the right bloc, mainly Likud, through persuasion rather than turnout. Israeli evidence.

sources.citation: Garthwaite, C., & Moore, T. J. (2013). Can Celebrity Endorsements Affect Political Outcomes? Evidence from the 2008 US Democratic Presidential Primary. Journal of Law, Economics, and Organization 29(2): 355-384.
sources.checked: verified
sources.note: Oprah Winfrey's 2008 endorsement of Obama is estimated to have added about a million primary votes. US evidence.

sources.citation: Carney, K. (2022, 16 Aug). The WhatsApp effect: Evidence on political engagement, preferences and polarisation. Ideas for India (summary of the working paper 'The Effect of Social Media on Voters: Experimental Evidence from an Indian Election').
sources.checked: verified. The party was assigned at random, and Tamil Nadu politics is less divisive than elsewhere.
sources.note: Tamil Nadu 2021: joining a party's WhatsApp group raised political knowledge and moved moderate voters toward the party without raising hostility. Posts from other members mattered more than the party's own posts. Foreign evidence.

sources.citation: Pasquetto, I. V., Jahani, E., Atreja, S., & Baum, M. (2022). Social Debunking of Misinformation on WhatsApp: The Case for Strong and In-group Ties. Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction 6(CSCW1), Article 117.
sources.checked: verified. Outcomes are survey measures of interest, belief and stated resharing, not observed forwarding.
sources.note: WhatsApp users in India and Pakistan were more likely to reshare a debunk from a close contact or someone who shared their politics. Audio debunks worked better than text or images.

sources.citation: Badrinathan, S. (2021). Educative Interventions to Combat Misinformation: Evidence from a Field Experiment in India. American Political Science Review 115(4): 1325-1341.
sources.checked: verified
sources.note: India 2019: an hour of media-literacy training did not improve people's ability to spot false stories, and ruling-party supporters got worse at spotting false stories that favoured their side.

sources.citation: Roozenbeek, J., van der Linden, S., Goldberg, B., Rathje, S., & Lewandowsky, S. (2022). Psychological inoculation improves resilience against misinformation on social media. Science Advances 8(34): eabo6254.
sources.checked: corrected: the 18 hours is a median, not a mean. Only two of the five technique videos were tested on YouTube, and the field effect narrowly missed the preregistered threshold.
sources.note: Short videos explaining manipulation techniques improved recognition of them in six lab studies and, as YouTube ads, by about 5% in the field, at about $0.05 per 30-second view. US evidence.

sources.citation: Modirrousta-Galian, A., & Higham, P. A. (2023). Gamified inoculation interventions do not improve discrimination between true and fake news: Reanalyzing existing research with receiver operating characteristic analysis. Journal of Experimental Psychology: General 152(9): 2411-2437.
sources.checked: corrected: the result holds where comparable true and false items were used. The statement that replications show the same pattern has no source and is dropped.
sources.note: A reanalysis of five studies found that inoculation games did not improve people's ability to tell true from false news. They made players more sceptical of all news. Foreign evidence.

sources.citation: Walter, N., Cohen, J., Holbert, R. L., & Morag, Y. (2020). Fact-Checking: A Meta-Analysis of What Works and for Whom. Political Communication 37(3): 350-375.
sources.checked: verified
sources.note: Meta-analysis of 30 studies: fact-checks improve the accuracy of political beliefs, least for campaign statements and among people whose prior beliefs they challenge. Foreign evidence.

sources.citation: Nyhan, B., Porter, E., Reifler, J., & Wood, T. J. (2020). Taking Fact-Checks Literally But Not Seriously? The Effects of Journalistic Fact-Checking on Factual Beliefs and Candidate Favorability. Political Behavior 42(3): 939-960.
sources.checked: verified
sources.note: US 2016: fact-checks of Trump's claims made beliefs more accurate, including among his supporters, but did not change support for him.

sources.citation: Berinsky, A. J. (2017). Rumors and Health Care Reform: Experiments in Political Misinformation. British Journal of Political Science 47(2): 241-262.
sources.checked: corrected: in the full sample the three corrections did not differ significantly (58% Republican, 57% nonpartisan and 54% Democratic source rejecting the rumour). The Republican-source correction stood out only among attentive respondents (69% against 60%). The figures first quoted came from a re-interviewed subset. The Republican correction stayed the most effective a week later.
sources.note: US experiments on the 'death panels' rumour: repeating a rumour increases belief in it, and corrections from an unexpected partisan source work best among attentive people.

sources.citation: Grinberg, N., Joseph, K., Friedland, L., Swire-Thompson, B., & Lazer, D. (2019). Fake news on Twitter during the 2016 U.S. presidential election. Science 363(6425): 374-378.
sources.checked: verified
sources.note: US 2016: fake-news sources were about 6% of political news consumption on Twitter, and 1% of users accounted for 80% of exposures.

sources.citation: Dobber, T., Metoui, N., Trilling, D., Helberger, N., & de Vreese, C. (2021). Do (Microtargeted) Deepfakes Have Real Effects on Political Attitudes? International Journal of Press/Politics 26(1): 69-91.
sources.checked: verified. The targeted subgroup is very small.
sources.note: Dutch experiment with 278 people: a deepfake video lowered attitudes toward the politician shown but not toward his party, except in the small subgroup it targeted.

sources.citation: Stockwell, S., et al. (2024, Nov). AI-Enabled Influence Operations: Safeguarding Future Elections. Centre for Emerging Technology and Security, The Alan Turing Institute. Also: Stockwell, S., et al. (2024, May). AI-Enabled Influence Operations: The Threat to the UK General Election. Summarised in The Alan Turing Institute's written evidence RGE 11 to the UK Parliament.
sources.checked: corrected: the figure of 112 elections with AI-enabled interference in 19 comes from the May 2024 briefing, not the November 2024 report. The parliament page blocks automated access, and its wording was confirmed from search results.
sources.note: The Alan Turing Institute found no conclusive evidence that AI-generated disinformation changed any 2024 election result, but warns of confusion about what is real and lower trust in online sources.

sources.citation: Knesset (1959, consolidated text as amended to 2026). Elections (Propaganda Methods) Law, 5719-1959. Hebrew Wikisource consolidation, with section 16 as published by the Central Elections Committee (2022). Sections cited: 2, 2A, 2A1, 2A2, 2B, 2C, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9, 10, 10A, 10B, 15, 15A, 16, 16E and 17.
sources.checked: corrected: the text matches on every point checked. Fixes in use: the written-consent rule for images covers only security-forces members wounded or killed because of their service and victims of hostile action (or their families), not any soldier. Separately, propaganda may not suggest the IDF is linked to a list, and the committee treats IDF uniforms as public property. The rest-day exclusion applies to TV broadcasts only. The poll-disclosure duty for broadcasts binds the first broadcaster and anyone re-broadcasting within 24 hours. France's poll blackout now covers only the eve and day of the vote. A claimed 2019 Likud election-day gift case could not be sourced and is not used.
sources.note: The propaganda rules: free TV and radio broadcasts only in the final 14 days (TV not on rest days), no other broadcast propaganda for 60 days, and every ad must name who commissioned it. Propaganda may never come with gifts or entertainment, and may come with food or alcohol only at gatherings in private homes. Posters go only on designated boards. Published polls must give their method, and no new poll results may be published from the end of Friday 23 October until polls close.

sources.citation: Ravia, H., & Hammer, D. (2026, 30 Jul). Israel Issues Deepfake Disclosure Rules for Election Campaign Publications. Pearl Cohen Zedek Latzer Baratz (client alert), summarising the Central Elections Committee's rules of 26 July 2026 under section 2A2 of the Elections (Propaganda Methods) Law.
sources.checked: verified
sources.note: From 23 July 2026, election propaganda that is a deepfake must carry a clear disclosure: on screen for the whole of a video at 5% of the screen or more, and read aloud at the start and end of audio. Every ad must also name who commissioned it.

sources.citation: Times of Israel (2026, 6 Aug). Elections panel orders Eisenkot to take down AI campaign video showing IDF soldiers (liveblog). The Times of Israel. Also: Israel National News (2026, 26 Jul). Precedential ruling against AI election ads.
sources.checked: verified. A NIS 8,500 legal-costs figure in the February case rests on one secondary source and is not used.
sources.note: The committee ordered Likud (February 2026) and Smotrich's RZP (July) to remove manipulated images linking change-bloc leaders with Arab leaders, and ordered Eisenkot (August) to remove a video with AI-generated soldiers. It held that an AI caption users are unlikely to notice is not enough.

sources.citation: Surkes, S. (2019, 14 Mar). Facebook rolls out political ad transparency less than a month before polls. The Times of Israel. Also: Google (n.d.). Israel election ads verification (Advertising Policies Help).
sources.checked: corrected: Google's Israel election-ads verification (since June 2020) is sourced to Google's help pages, not the article. Per-ad audience breakdowns by age, gender and region are a current Meta Ad Library feature that the article does not describe.
sources.note: The committee chair banned anonymous online election ads from March 2019, and since 2022 the law requires every ad to name who commissioned it. Facebook verifies political advertisers and keeps their ads in a public library for seven years.

sources.citation: Benjakob, O. (2026, 12 Sep). The Money Race: How Much Israeli Politicians Are Spending on Online Ads. Haaretz.
sources.checked: verified. Spending figures are behind a paywall and were not retrieved.
sources.note: For nearly three years Likud barely used Meta ads and campaigned through WhatsApp groups and a Telegram chatbot that leave no public record. It resumed paid Facebook advertising in late August 2026 and quickly outspent most rivals.

sources.citation: State Comptroller of Israel (2026, July). The National Response to Foreign Influence in the Digital Space (Hebrew), special report. Office of the State Comptroller. Also: The Times of Israel (2021, 30 Nov) on the Comptroller's 2019-elections findings.
sources.checked: verified. Only parts of the report were published, for security reasons. A report that the Shin Bet chief named Iran as the main foreign actor in 2026 was not re-checked and is not used.
sources.note: Israel still has no national policy on foreign digital influence, nine years after the threat was identified. Iran and Hezbollah sent about 5 million hostile text messages in September 2024. The report urges the committee to prepare before the 2026 election.

sources.citation: Shwartz Altshuler, T., & Sapozhnikova, I. O. (2024, 26 May). Media and Social Media Consumption, Trust, and Literacy. Israel Democracy Institute (Jewish sample).
sources.checked: verified
sources.note: Among Jewish Israelis, Channel 12 is the main TV news source (51%) and Channel 14 second (20%, almost all on the right). 65% get news through WhatsApp, and family and friends' groups are trusted more than groups run by politicians or journalists.

sources.citation: ICE news site (2026, 10 Apr). Evening news ratings, Thursday 9 April 2026 (Hebrew). ice.co.il.
sources.checked: corrected: the source reports viewers on one sampled night, not households.
sources.note: On one April 2026 night, Channel 12's evening news drew about 411,000 viewers, Channel 14 about 223,000 and Channel 13 about 145,000.

sources.citation: Wiener, A., & Stegman, O. (2024, 21 Apr). Social Media and Digital Platform Use in Israel (2024). Israel Internet Association.
sources.checked: corrected: Arab adults' Telegram use is 66%, with only 28% using it daily, against 43% daily for all adults. The 2025 figures attributed to the Jerusalem Post could not be found and are not used.
sources.note: Almost all Israeli adults use WhatsApp (98%) and YouTube, Facebook reaches 87%, and Telegram rose to 70% in 2024. Instagram and TikTok dominate among 18-22-year-olds, and 71% of Arab adults use TikTok.

sources.citation: NEWSru.co.il (2024, 23 Jan). Media and social networks of Russian-speaking Israelis during the war: poll results (Russian). NEWSru.co.il.
sources.checked: verified. A self-selected reader poll, so low confidence.
sources.note: A large reader poll of Russian-speaking Israelis (January 2024): news sites dominate, Channel 9 is the most-watched TV channel, and use of Russian-language Telegram channels for war news more than doubled after October 7.

sources.citation: Yarchi, M., Baden, C., & Kligler-Vilenchik, N. (2021). Political Polarization on the Digital Sphere: A Cross-platform, Over-time Analysis of Interactional, Positional, and Affective Polarization on Social Media. Political Communication 38(1-2): 98-139.
sources.checked: verified. Facebook was the least homophilic of the three platforms.
sources.note: One Israeli controversy over 16 months (about 250,000 posts): Twitter showed growing polarisation and hostility, while WhatsApp discussion became less polarised over time.

sources.citation: Aridor Hershkowitz, R., & Shwartz Altshuler, T. (2026, 6 Oct). Wrongful blocking of WhatsApp accounts during elections: potential consequences and the need for early preparation and a fast-track review mechanism (Hebrew). Israel Democracy Institute position paper, with Ori Grodzinsky.
sources.checked: corrected: the paper does not say WhatsApp told parties it is not for messaging at scale, or that Brazil banned mass political messaging. It reports that WhatsApp bans over 2 million accounts a month for bulk or automated messaging, that Brazil's electoral court and Meta run a channel for flagging mass electoral messaging, and that about ten Yesh Atid MKs' accounts were blocked in September 2023.

sources.citation: Duch, R. M., May, J., & Armstrong, D. A. (2010). Coalition-directed Voting in Multiparty Democracies. American Political Science Review 104(4): 698-719.
sources.checked: corrected: the surveys span a 25-year period, not more than 25 years.
sources.note: 86 surveys in 23 countries: voters anticipate the policy deals coalition partners will strike, and coalition-directed voting is common wherever coalition government is the norm.

sources.citation: Meffert, M. F., & Gschwend, T. (2010). Strategic coalition voting: Evidence from Austria. Electoral Studies 29(3): 339-349.
sources.checked: corrected: the paper finds only some evidence that coalition preferences and uncertainty interact, not that every mechanism depends on both. Loan votes appear among supporters of the big centre-right party who were unsure whether its junior partner would pass, and coalition-shaping votes among Green supporters unsure of a Social Democrat-Green majority.
sources.note: Austria 2006: supporters of big parties lent votes to an at-risk junior partner, and small-party supporters avoided wasted votes. Insincere voting was about 4% among supporters of the two big parties and 11-23% among smaller parties' supporters. Foreign evidence.

sources.citation: Gschwend, T., Meffert, M. F., & Stoetzer, L. F. (2017). Weighting Parties and Coalitions: How Coalition Signals Influence Voting Behavior. The Journal of Politics 79(2): 642-655.
sources.checked: verified. Magnitudes from the authors' online appendix: after a coalition signal, 9-11% (Austria) and 19-20% (Germany) of respondents switched party in the vignette.
sources.note: Survey experiments in Austria and Germany: explicit signals about desirable and undesirable coalitions make voters weigh coalition considerations more and party loyalty less. Some change their vote as a result.

sources.citation: Bahnsen, O., Stoetzer, L. F., & Gschwend, T. (2025). Coalition-Directed Voting Under Uncertainty. The Journal of Politics (published online 29 April 2025).
sources.checked: corrected: the vignette experiment found risk aversion for the CDU/CSU but no clear effect for the Greens, so the causal finding is partial. Effect sizes are now extracted: across 17 pre-election studies in seven countries, moving a party's coalition prospects from least to most uncertain lowers its vote probability by about 11 points.
sources.note: Voters are less likely to back a party whose coalition prospects look uncertain, even when the expected outcome is the same. Evidence from seven countries, not Israel.

sources.citation: Falcó-Gimeno, A., & Muñoz, J. (2017). Show Me Your Friends: A Survey Experiment on the Effect of Coalition Signals. The Journal of Politics 79(4): 1454-1459.
sources.checked: corrected: the sample was 1,003, and honesty was not measured in the published article. Only right-leaning signals moved where respondents placed the parties (about half a point on a 0-10 scale). Left-leaning or rule-out signals did not. The study supports the idea that a rightward signal repositions a party, not that a leftward one does.
sources.note: Valencia 2015 survey experiment: coalition signals shifted expectations and the perceived position of parties, especially a new party. Foreign evidence.

sources.citation: Bäck, H., Hellström, J., Lindvall, J., & Teorell, J. (2024). Pre-electoral coalitions, familiarity, and delays in government formation. West European Politics 47(1): 88-112.
sources.checked: verified
sources.note: 17 West European democracies (1945-2019): pre-electoral blocs that fall short of a majority can delay government formation rather than speed it up, as in Sweden in 2018-19.

sources.citation: Ansolabehere, S. D., Snyder, J. M., Jr., Strauss, A. B., & Ting, M. M. (2005). Voting Weights and Formateur Advantages in the Formation of Coalition Governments. American Journal of Political Science 49(3): 550-563.
sources.checked: verified
sources.note: Coalition governments 1946-2001: partners get cabinet posts in proportion to their voting weight, while the party that forms the government gets a substantial bonus.

sources.citation: Strøm, K. (1984). Minority Governments in Parliamentary Democracies: The Rationality of Nonwinning Cabinet Solutions. Comparative Political Studies 17(2): 199-227.
sources.checked: corrected: minority cabinets were about 35% of governments, not roughly a third.
sources.note: Minority governments are common and rational, about 35% of post-war cabinets in 15 democracies. They form when opposition parties can still shape policy and governing is expected to cost votes.

sources.citation: Krauss, S., & Thürk, M. (2022). Stability of minority governments and the role of support agreements. West European Politics 45(4): 767-792.
sources.checked: verified. From the online appendix: minority cabinets without agreements face roughly 1.4-2 times the risk of early termination, while those with written support agreements are as stable as majority cabinets.
sources.note: 471 cabinets in 30 countries: minority governments backed by written support agreements last about as long as majority governments. Those without agreements fall much sooner.

sources.citation: Klüver, H., & Spoon, J.-J. (2020). Helping or Hurting? How Governing as a Junior Coalition Partner Influences Electoral Outcomes. The Journal of Politics 82(4): 1231-1242.
sources.checked: verified. The abstract gives no magnitude, and a '6% fewer votes' figure from a later paper could not be checked, so it is not used.
sources.note: 307 parties in 28 European countries (1972-2017): serving as a junior coalition partner considerably hurts a party at the next election. Ra'am's gain in 2022 is a counter-example.

sources.citation: Fortunato, D. (2019). The Electoral Implications of Coalition Policy Making. British Journal of Political Science 49(1): 59-80.
sources.checked: verified
sources.note: Six parliamentary democracies: voters punish parties they see as compromising in coalition and discount their achievements.

sources.checked: corrected: the article is open access and the numbers are now extracted. Pooled, the mailer raised turnout by 1.0 point, mostly among voters with a 20-60% prior chance of voting, with no effect above 60%. Subjects were about 650,000 likely Democratic supporters chosen by a progressive group.
sources.note: Wisconsin 2012 recall: the 'Neighbors' social-pressure mailer raised turnout by 1 point in a hotly contested election, against 8 points in a low-salience primary. It had no effect on voters who usually vote.

sources.citation: Panagopoulos, C., Larimer, C. W., & Condon, M. (2014). Social Pressure, Descriptive Norms, and Voter Mobilization. Political Behavior 36(2): 451-469.
sources.checked: verified
sources.note: US field experiment: social-pressure mail worked only when it showed recipients' own vote history. Community turnout rates or 'everyone votes' messages alone did little.

sources.citation: Gerber, A. S., Huber, G. A., & Fang, A. H. (2023). Voting behavior is unaffected by subtle linguistic cues: Evidence from a psychologically authentic replication. Behavioural Public Policy 7(2): 380-394.
sources.checked: verified. There were two earlier large replications with no effect: Gerber, Huber, Biggers and Hendry (2016, PNAS) and Gerber, Huber and Fang (2018, Political Psychology).
sources.note: A large preregistered replication in the 2016 US election found no effect of calling people 'voters' instead of asking them to vote, against 11-14 points claimed in small early studies.

sources.citation: Jones, J. J., Bond, R. M., Bakshy, E., Eckles, D., & Fowler, J. H. (2017). Social influence and political mobilization: Further evidence from a randomized experiment in the 2012 U.S. presidential election. PLoS ONE 12(4): e0173851.
sources.checked: verified. About 15 million is the matched analysis sample, not the number of users shown the message.
sources.note: US election day 2012: Facebook's 'I voted' message raised validated turnout by about 0.24 points among 15 million matched users, and friends' turnout rose by about twice the direct effect.

sources.citation: Haenschen, K. (2016). Social Pressure on Social Media: Using Facebook Status Updates to Increase Voter Turnout. Journal of Communication 66(4): 542-563.
sources.checked: verified. Group turnout rates for the first study come from secondary coverage, and the senders were local Democratic activists.
sources.note: Three small US experiments: tagging friends in Facebook posts that revealed whether they had voted raised turnout substantially. Low confidence, small samples.

sources.citation: Green, D. P., & McClellan, O. A. (2020). Turnout Nation: A Pilot Experiment Evaluating a Get-Out-The-Vote 'Supertreatment'. Working paper, Columbia University.
sources.checked: verified. The programme was nonpartisan and captains were told not to mention parties, so a partisan captain programme is a different, untested treatment.
sources.note: US pilot (2019 municipal elections): volunteer 'captains' each listed about 20 friends and neighbours, and the random half they were asked to mobilise voted 13 points more than the other half, the largest effect in two decades of experiments. A small, low-salience, nonpartisan pilot.

sources.citation: Gerber, A., Hoffman, M., Morgan, J., & Raymond, C. (2020). One in a Million: Field Experiments on Perceived Closeness of the Election and Voter Turnout. American Economic Journal: Applied Economics 12(3): 287-325.
sources.checked: verified
sources.note: US field experiments: showing voters a close poll changed their beliefs about closeness but not their turnout. Effects above 0.8 points are ruled out.

sources.citation: Enos, R. D., & Fowler, A. (2014). Pivotality and Turnout: Evidence from a Field Experiment in the Aftermath of a Tied Election. Political Science Research and Methods 2(2): 309-319.
sources.checked: verified

sources.checked: verified. These are two-option referenda, where closeness is unambiguous.
sources.note: Swiss referenda: a closer published poll raised turnout by about 1.2 points over three days, mostly for the trailing side. Foreign evidence.

sources.checked: verified
sources.note: French overseas territories that voted after mainland exit polls were public: turnout was about 11 points lower, and the remaining voters leaned toward the expected winner.

sources.checked: verified. The specific percentages come from the authors' published response to critics, not the article.
sources.note: US experiments: win-probability forecasts make a race look more decided than vote-share projections and can lower turnout, mostly among the leader's supporters.

sources.checked: verified
sources.note: Lab experiments: publishing polls raised the expected majority's turnout and produced more lopsided results. Foreign lab evidence.

sources.checked: verified

Donation caps differ by party: NIS 2,800 per household in an election year for a represented party, five times that (NIS 14,000) for a party not represented in the outgoing Knesset, and up to NIS 28,000 for a seatless list in the 12 months after the vote to pay debts. For outside bodies, the duty to incorporate and appoint an auditor applies only above NIS 481,600, and no Knesset candidate or holder of any party role may hold a senior role in them. A list above 1% with no seats is owed one unit, which mostly reduces the advance it must repay.
sources.note: Campaign finance rules: state funding and spending caps counted in financing units (NIS 1.835 million each for this election), donations only from individual voters with household caps, and one unit for lists that win over 1% but no seats. Outside groups spending over NIS 120,400 on election activity must register and publish their donations.

sources.note: Parties get the voter register only for election use and may not pass it on (misuse carries up to 2 years). The Privacy Protection Authority requires databases built on it to have need-based access, two-factor login, logs and vendor contracts, and to be deleted after the election, including at vendors.

sources.note: US field experiments with civic groups: a message tied to members' own goals almost tripled petition signing, a new-member framing about tripled recruiting, and a debrief conversation raised meeting attendance from about 13% to 42%. The figures come from a practitioner summary of the article.

sources.checked: corrected: the paper finds that standard management tools did not fix the problem, so it supports choosing representative messengers rather than tighter scripts.
sources.note: Obama 2012 field workers were demographically unrepresentative and ideologically extreme, and misjudged voters' priorities. The campaign could not correct this with standard management tools.
